As laid out by Grandi [32], four mechanisms are commonly explored to explain the origin of O i $\lambda 8449$ emission: O+ recombination, collisional excitation by free electrons, continuum fluorescence, and Bowen [10] fluorescence from Ly $\beta$ (also referred to as Ly $\beta$ pumping or a PAR process; Bhatia and Kastner 9). It has been noted [65, e.g.,] that several processes can simultaneously contribute to O i production in an individual object, complicating the interpretation of simple diagnostics such as those presented by Grandi [32]. With this consideration in mind, we aim to identify the dominant mechanism powering O i emission in our sample by quantifying the contribution of each of these processes to the O i $\lambda 8449$ feature. In this Section, we primarily compare predicted line ratios for each excitation mechanism with the emission-line measurements in the Stack-Det composite spectrum. Firstly, its superior signal-to-noise ratio enables a robust comparison between the observed and predicted line ratios for each excitation mechanism. Secondly, the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratios in both Stack-Det and Stack-NonDet are consistent within 1 $\sigma$ , strongly suggesting that the same excitation mechanism produces O i $\lambda 8449$ emission in both composite samples, and thus characterizing the Stack-Det composite is sufficient. We explore each of the four aforementioned mechanisms in the following subsections, ultimately finding that the stellar continuum fluorescence mechanism is most consistent with our observations.

### IV.1 Recombination

The recombination of free electrons with O+ ions should produce emission-line features arising from cascades down various transition pathways of the O0 atom. Such features include the O i $\lambda 7776$ quintet $(\rm 3s\ ^{5}S-3p\ ^{5}P)$ , and not only lines produced by the transition pathways that lead to the emission of O i $\lambda 8449$ . In the case of recombination, the ratio of O i $\lambda 7776$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ is expected to be roughly 5/3, based upon the ratio of the statistical weights of the O i $\lambda 7776$ quintet and O i $\lambda 8449$ triplet [32]. Given that O i $\lambda 7776$ emission is not detected in any of the galaxies in the AURORA sample analyzed here, and all upper limits place the O i $\lambda 7776$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio below unity, the recombination mechanism is unlikely to be a significant contributor to the O i emission for any object in this sample.

We estimate the contribution of recombination to the O i $\lambda 8449$ flux by using the expressions for the recombination volume emission coefficients of O i $\lambda 8449$ and H $\beta$ from Grandi [31]. From these equations, we can derive an expression for the expected ratio of O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\beta$ :

$$ \frac{j_{8449}}{j_{H\beta}}=\left(\frac{N_{\rm OII}}{N_{\rm HII}}\right)\times\left(\frac{\nu_{8449}}{\nu_{\rm H\beta}}\right)\times 6.84\times T_{4}^{0.22} $$

where $T_{4}$ is the electron temperature in units of $10^{4}$ K, and $N_{\rm OII}$ and $N_{\rm HII}$ are the O+ and H+ number densities, respectively. Using the PyNeb package [52], we calculate $T_{4}$ and $\rm O^{+}/H^{+}$ based on the Stack-Det composite emission-line measurements. Based on the stacked, temperature-sensitive [O ii] $\lambda\lambda 3727,3730$ /[O ii] $\lambda\lambda 7322,7332$ ratio, we derive an electron temperature in the O+ zone of $T_{e}$ ([O ii]) $=13,696\pm 750$ K, adopting a density of $n_{e}=442\pm 88\rm\ cm^{-3}$ based on the density-sensitive [S ii] $\lambda 6733$ /[S ii] $\lambda 6718$ ratio. Using these values of $T_{e}$ and $n_{e}$ , we derive an O+/H+ abundance of $(3.603\pm 0.725)\times 10^{-5}$ . Adopting these values, and assuming an intrinsic Balmer decrement of H $\alpha$ /H $\beta=2.79$ to convert to a ratio with respect to H $\alpha$ , we predict log(O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha)=-4.26\pm 0.08$ , more than an order of magnitude lower than the values that are typical of our sample. Taking the ratio of the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ value vs. the measured value from the stack, we estimate that recombination contributes $1.0\pm 0.2$ % to the stacked O i $\lambda 8449$ flux. This percentage is likely an upper limit, since the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio inferred from equation 1 is based on the assumption that the spatial distribution of O+ and H+ are the same, when in reality, O+ occupies a smaller volume of a typical H ii region than H+ [28, e.g.,]. In summary, recombination is unlikely to be a significant contributor to the observed O i $\lambda 8449$ emission.

### IV.2 Collisional excitation

Another proposed excitation mechanism is the population of the 3p $\rm{}^{3}P$ level by collisions between free electrons and O0 atoms. Grandi [32] explored signatures of collisionally excited O i $\lambda 8449$ , noting that for this mechanism, one would expect the ratio of O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449$ to be $\sim$ 0.3, assuming an electron temperature of 10,000 K and adopting the collisional cross sections compiled by Haisch et al. [35]. Bhatia and Kastner [9] carried out a more detailed analysis of the oxygen atom, computing effective collision strengths in a 13-level atomic model with 66 transitions, presenting line-strength predictions as a function of temperature and density. Utilizing the effective collision strengths from Bhatia and Kastner, we calculate an expected ratio of O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449=0.55\pm 0.01$ using the PyNeb package, adopting the $T_{e}$ and $n_{e}$ derived in Section IV.1. We show the predicted O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio as a function of $T_{e}$ and $n_{e}$ in the top panel of Figure 5. O i $\lambda 7776$ is not detected in any object or stack from the AURORA sample. Five of the objects in this sample, as well as both stacks, yield upper limits on O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449$ lower than 0.55. The Stack-NonDet composite yields an upper limit of $<$ 0.54, which, formally, does not rule out collisional excitation for the non-detections. However, given that the upper limit on O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449$ is $<$ 0.09 in the Stack-Det composite, collisional excitation is unlikely to be the dominant contributor to O i $\lambda 8449$ emission in the AURORA galaxies.

*Figure 5: Oxygen line ratio predictions from PyNeb. Measurements from the Stack-Det composite are shaded in gray. (Top) Predicted O i $\lambda 7776/$ O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio vs. $n_{e}$ and $T_{e}$ . (Bottom) [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio vs. $n_{e}$ and $T_{e}$ .*

A more informative constraint on collisional excitation is obtained by interpreting the ratio of the forbidden [O i] $\lambda 6302$ line to O i $\lambda 8449$ . Because the upper level of the [O i] $\lambda 6302$ transition ( $\rm 2p^{4}\ {}^{1}D_{2}$ ) lies at a relatively low energy (1.967 eV), this line is easily collisionally excited in the outskirts of H ii regions, given the typical range of temperatures observed. If we assume that collisional excitation is responsible for 100% of the [O i] emission, and that [O i] $\lambda 6302$ and O i $\lambda 8449$ arise from the same gas, then the [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio serves as a valuable constraint on the collisional excitation of the O0 atom.

Based on the $T_{e}$ and $n_{e}$ values derived in Section IV.1, the inferred ratio of [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ is $3200\pm 1700$ , adopting the collision strengths from Bhatia and Kastner [9]. This value lies significantly above the ratios measured in all individual objects in the AURORA sample as well as the stack. To demonstrate the range of ISM conditions required to reproduce the observed [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ in our sample, we show this ratio as a function of $T_{e}$ and $n_{e}$ in the bottom panel of Figure 5. To reproduce the observed stacked [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio at typical ISM densities requires an electron temperature of 100,000 K, in extreme excess of plausible temperatures in even the hottest portions of H ii regions. To reproduce the [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio at more plausible H ii region temperatures, one must infer a density of $n_{e}\gtrsim 10^{8}\ \rm cm^{-3}$ , in excess of what is typically measured in H ii regions and PDRs [37, 83, 78, 38, e.g.,]. Thus, to produce the O i $\lambda 8449$ line with collisional excitation, one must assume implausibly extreme ISM conditions. We note that the [O i] $\lambda 6302$ line can be enhanced by shocks, in addition to collisional excitation [88, e.g.,]. However, accounting for shock-enhanced [O i] would only decrease the fraction of our measured [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio that is produced by collisional excitation, making the ratio more difficult to reproduce with collisions. Comparison of the [O i] $\lambda 6302$ /O i $\lambda 8449=3200\pm 1700$ ratio with our observed ratio from the stack suggests that collisional excitation contributes only $0.16\pm 0.09$ % to the Stack-Det O i $\lambda 8449$ emission.

### IV.3 Ly $\beta$ fluorescence

The remaining processes, stellar continuum and Ly $\beta$ fluorescence, are expected to produce distinct patterns of O i emission-line ratios. A key indicator to distinguish between these two mechanisms is the strength of the O i $\lambda 11290$ line. In the case of Ly $\beta$ fluorescence, O i $\lambda 11290$ is expected to have an equal photon flux to O i $\lambda 8449$ , since every transition from 3d $\rm{}^{3}D^{\circ}$ to 3p $\rm{}^{3}P$ (in the absence of other lines populating the 3p $\rm{}^{3}P$ level) results in a subsequent emission of an O i $\lambda 8449$ photon. This condition of equal photon flux thus sets a theoretical flux ratio of O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 8449=0.749$ . However, the observed ratio or upper limit of O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ in the stacks is significantly lower than the ratio predicted from Ly $\beta$ fluorescence. Furthermore, in individual objects, the 3 detected O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratios are significantly lower than the Ly $\beta$ fluorescence prediction, and 8 out of 10 upper limits are below this prediction as well.

A quantitative estimate of the contribution of Ly $\beta$ PAR to the emission of O i $\lambda 8449$ can be found by following the analyses of Morgan [56] and Grandi [31]. To explain the O i $\lambda 8449$ emission in the Orion nebula, Grandi [31] derived this expression for the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio:22 2 Note: Grandi [31] originally provides the numerical values for this expression with respect to H $\beta$ , having converted from H $\alpha$ using an unreported value for the Balmer decrement. We have re-expressed this equation here, assuming H $\alpha$ /H $\beta=2.79$

$$ \frac{F_{8449}}{F_{\rm H\alpha}}=1.97\times 10^{-4}\left(\frac{\rm O/H}{6\times 10^{-4}}\right) $$

This expression is obtained by integrating the volume emission coefficients for O i $\lambda 8449$ and H $\alpha$ over an idealized model of Orion, and assuming that Ly $\beta$ PAR is the only excitation mechanism for O i $\lambda 8449$ . Grandi also notes that the derivation of this ratio assumes that H $\alpha$ photons are only produced by the decay of Ly $\beta$ into H $\alpha$ and Ly $\alpha$ , and thus the prediction should be interpreted as an upper limit. Adopting an oxygen abundance of $\rm O/H=(1.28\pm 0.12)\times 10^{-4}$ for Stack-Det based on the physical conditions calculated in Section IV.1, we predict log(O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha)=-4.38\pm 0.04$ , which is similar to that derived for the case of recombination in Section IV.1. This argument predicts that Ly $\beta$ fluorescence would only contribute $0.81\pm 0.08\%$ to the observed O i $\lambda 8449$ emission in Stack-Det.

Grandi [32] also calculated the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio in the context of the broad-line region in AGN, yielding a value of log(O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha)=-2.82$ , a much closer match to the values that we observe in AURORA. However, producing such strong O i $\lambda 8449$ emission through Ly $\beta$ fluorescence requires extreme conditions, namely a very high optical depth to H $\alpha$ photons. As Grandi [32] notes, Ly $\beta$ photons are converted to H $\alpha$ quickly after $\sim$ 10 scatterings, while $\sim$ $5\times 10^{4}$ scatterings are required before Ly $\beta$ will encounter an oxygen atom and excite it to the 3d $\rm\ {}^{3}D^{\circ}$ state. As a result, H $\alpha$ must be optically thick ( $\tau_{\rm H\alpha}\sim 7\times 10^{4}$ ) to retain enough Ly $\beta$ photons within the nebula for the PAR process to be efficient. It is unlikely that this condition is satisfied in the majority of H ii regions such that the O i $\lambda 8449$ line is measured at the strength we observe in both composite stacks comprising 58 star-forming galaxies as well as the 1602 galaxies from the DESI survey. As such, we rule out this mechanism as a significant contributor to O i $\lambda 8449$ emission. With Ly $\beta$ fluorescence ruled out, we explore the remaining mechanism: stellar continuum fluorescence.

### IV.4 Stellar continuum fluorescence

Qualitatively, a proposed indicator of stellar continuum fluorescence of O i $\lambda 8449$ is the presence of O i $\lambda 13168$ emission that is stronger than $\lambda 11290$ , but weaker than $\lambda 8449$ , i.e., O i $\lambda 8449>$ O i $\lambda 13168>$ O i $\lambda 11290$ [31, 69, e.g.,]. This trend is borne out in the majority of the AURORA O i sample as well as the stacks. For a quantitative comparison, we analyze the emission-line predictions performed by Grandi [31] for an idealized model of the Orion nebula. For the case of continuum fluorescence, Grandi [31] predicts an O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\beta$ ratio of 0.009 which, assuming an intrinsic Balmer decrement of H $\alpha$ /H $\beta=2.86$ , yields an O i strength of log(O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha)=-2.50$ , consistent with the distribution of O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ values observed in the AURORA sample as well as CHAOS and DESI. Grandi [31] also predicts a O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio of 0.33, and a O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio of 0.022 for Orion. The O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ prediction is in good agreement with the Stack-Det composite, and lower than, but the same order of magnitude as the Stack-NonDet composite. The O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ prediction is much smaller than the observed value in our stack as well as the three individual objects with detections, possibly suggestive of the need for a more sophisticated model to account for this line ratio. Despite the small differences between the Grandi [31] predictions and our observations, this comparison suggests that stellar continuum fluorescence is the most compelling explanation for the O i $\lambda 8449$ emission.

### IV.5 Cloudy photoionization modeling

To provide an independent set of predictions of the O i line strengths, we model a mock H ii region and surrounding neutral ISM using Cloudy [34]. We utilize a spherical H ii-region model, fixing the gas-phase oxygen abundance to a value of $\rm 12+\log(O/H)=8.11$ , as derived from the Stack-Det-based physical conditions presented in Section IV.1. Another input to the Cloudy model is the ionization parameter, $\log(U)$ . We derive this parameter from the Stack-Det composite using the empirical relationship between $\log(U)$ , $\rm 12+log(O/H)$ , and dust-corrected [O iii] $\lambda 5008$ /[O ii] $\lambda\lambda 3727,3730$ from Kewley et al. [45]. For this calculation, based on the inferred $n_{e}$ and $T_{e}$ , we assume $\log(P/k)=7.0$ and derive a value for the ionization parameter of $\log(U)=-2.72$ . We fix the ionization parameter to this value in the Cloudy simulation. We irradiate the cloud using the Binary Population and Stellar Synthesis [25, 74, BPASS;] v2.2.1 stellar population models, adopting a stellar age of 1 Myr, a stellar metallicity of $Z_{*}=0.001$ , and an upper IMF cutoff of $300\ M_{\odot}$ , including the effects of binary stars. We adopt an isobaric H ii-region model, varying the initial hydrogen density between $\log(\rm n_{H}/\rm cm^{-3})=[3,5]$ . In this setup, the converged model typically produces a density profile that is roughly constant within the H ii region, equal to the initialized density value, and sharply increases at the H ii region boundary into the neutral zone. We thus refer to the initialized density as the H ii-region density.

We additionally vary the ISM turbulence, since the kinematics of the gas in the ISM modulates the absorption line widths, thereby impacting the amount of continuum energy that is absorbed and re-emitted in the fluorescent lines. We vary this property between [1,50] km/s. To sufficiently extend the simulation into the neutral ISM where the bulk of O i emission originates, we set the cloud thickness to 2 pc, finding that this thickness sufficiently captures the extended O i emission profile. The Galactic cosmic-ray background from Indriolo et al. [39] is included in the simulation. To allow for transitions from higher energy levels that feed into the 3p 3P level (e.g., from 4s 3S∘, 5s 3S∘, 6s 3S∘, 7s 3S∘, 4d 3D∘, 5d 3D∘, and 6d 3D∘, as in Grandi 31), we include the lowest 100 energy levels of the O0 atom in the simulation, with the 100th level corresponding to the 6g $\rm{}^{3}G^{\circ}_{4}$ term. We show various resulting emission-line ratios in Figure 6.

The solid-line model curves show the Cloudy runs with a cosmic-ray background included, while the dotted-line model curves show models that exclude cosmic rays. Measurements from the Stack-Det spectrum are indicated by a gray dashed line, with the 1 $\sigma$ confidence interval shaded in gray. For comparison, the Grandi [31] observation and model predictions are shown as dotted and solid blue horizontal lines, respectively. Observations of the Orion bar from Walmsley et al. [84] are also shown for comparison as green dotted lines.*

In the top panel of Figure 6, we show the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio as a function of H ii-region density and ISM turbulence. Apart from the lowest densities, the range of turbulence values that we explore yields line-ratio predictions that are comparable to each other within $\sim$ 0.3 dex. Our Cloudy model predictions are largely consistent with the model prediction from Grandi [31] for the Orion nebula at $n_{e}=4000\rm\ cm^{-3}$ , shown as a solid dark blue line. Converting their reported measurement of O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\beta$ to O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ assuming H $\alpha$ /H $\beta=2.86$ (appropriate for a $T_{e}=10,000$ K nebula), we derive an O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ value for Orion (dark blue dotted line) that matches the Stack-Det value almost exactly. These similarities suggest similar processes may be at work in Orion and in the AURORA star-forming galaxies. For H ii-region densities of $\gtrsim$ 10 ${}^{3}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ , the Cloudy models predict log(O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha)>-2.75$ , with higher densities yielding better agreement with the observed Stack-Det value of $-2.28\pm 0.02$ .

Informed by the constraints from the [S ii] ratio presented in Section IV.1, adopting a value of $n_{\rm H}=10^{2.65}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ places Stack-Det in the density regime where model predictions fall short of the Stack-Det O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio. However, observations have demonstrated that the density structure of the ISM can vary greatly between indicators, with high-ionization density indicators such as the C iii] doublet yielding higher densities by over an order of magnitude compared to [S ii] [78, e.g.,]. Typically, in our simplified, isobaric H ii-region models, the density is roughly constant throughout the H ii region, only increasing significantly at the ionization front and into the surrounding neutral medium. Due to the non-trivial density structure of the ISM at $z\sim 2$ , a range of H ii-region densities can plausibly be considered for our simplistic model, and the H ii-region density does not necessarily have to match that derived from the [S ii] doublet.

If we adopt a density of $n_{\rm H}\gtrsim 10^{3.5}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ , consistent with that adopted by Grandi [31] for Orion, stellar continuum fluorescence can fully account for the observed O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio in the Stack-Det composite over a wide range of turbulence values. Given the uncertainties surrounding the effects of the H ii-region density structure on these results, future work employing more sophisticated H ii-region density profiles would prove as a valuable avenue to more robustly model O i $\lambda 8449$ emission. As an additional exercise, we explore the effects of varying the nebular oxygen abundance, finding that this parameter has a minimal impact on the predicted O i line ratios. The results of this exercise are shown in Appendix A.

In addition to the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio, we show predictions for the O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio in the middle panel of Figure 6. The Cloudy models shown in this Figure exhibit log(O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ) ratios that are smaller than the Stack-Det value of $-0.42\pm 0.06$ , differing by $\sim 0.1-0.5$ dex across a wide range of hydrogen densities and turbulence values. The Grandi [31] model prediction of log(O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449)=-0.48$ is closer to the observed Stack-Det ratio, differing by only $0.06\pm 0.06$ dex. We also examine the O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio, shown in the bottom panel of Figure 6. In the case of stellar continuum fluorescence, this ratio is predicted to be less than unity [31, 69]. Indeed, O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168<1$ in the Stack-Det composite. For turbulence values $>$ 1 km/s, Cloudy underpredicts the O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio, differing by $\sim$ 0.2–0.5 dex below the Stack-Det ratio at $\rm n_{H}\lesssim 10^{4}\ cm^{-3}$ . The discrepancy between Stack-Det and the ratio predicted by Grandi [31] is even larger, differing by $0.80\pm 0.10$ dex.

The O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio can be explained in the case of an H ii region with $n_{\rm H}=10^{2}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ and 1 km/s of turbulence. However, the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratios disfavor such a low H ii-region density. Adopting densities of $n_{\rm H}\gtrsim 10^{4}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ and $<$ 50 km/s of turbulence also yields O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratios that are close to the observed value. As such, the O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio suggests a density of $\sim$ $10^{4}-10^{5}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ , roughly consistent, though slightly higher than the densities one would infer based on the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio alone.

Walmsley et al. [84] measured values of log(O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168)=-0.14$ to $0.06$ for three pointings in the Orion Bar, exceeding the ratio predicted by Grandi [31] by an order of magnitude. For most combinations of turbulence and H ii-region density, the Cloudy models also predict a lower O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio than observed by Walmsley et al. [84]. The Cloudy models that best agree with these observations are characterized by either a low turbulence ( $\sim$ 1 km/s), or a high density at fixed turbulence. It is plausible to consider the possibility that the O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ ratio is higher in the Orion bar than in the $z\sim 2$ AURORA sample because the ISM at $z\sim 2$ is typically more turbulent than at $z\sim 0$ [27]. A valuable improvement on the Cloudy models would be to implement more realistic density and turbulence gradients in the simulated nebula, since both of these quantities can strongly influence O i $\lambda 11290$ /O i $\lambda 13168$ , and should accordingly be modeled in more careful detail. Future work focusing on such improvements will be necessary in order to fully understand O i production in star-forming galaxies.

In summary, comparing observed O i line ratios in AURORA and Orion with Cloudy models suggests that H ii-region densities in the range $\sim$ $10^{3.5}-10^{5}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ are necessary to explain the observations. Reproducing the observed O i $\lambda 13168$ /O i $\lambda 8449$ ratio remains a challenge, since no Cloudy models presented in this work match the observed ratio. This discrepancy may indicate the presence of additional physical considerations that are not currently captured by the models. However, compared to the other excitation mechanisms (i.e., recombination, collisional excitation, and Ly $\beta$ PAR), stellar continuum fluorescence is the most compelling in its ability to predict the observed O i line strengths.

## V Discussion

Stellar continuum fluorescence as a production mechanism for O i $\lambda 8449$ in the AURORA sample of star-forming galaxies has several interesting astrophysical implications. Firstly, we have ruled out Ly $\beta$ fluorescence as a dominant mechanism producing O i $\lambda 8449$ based on the observed strength of O i $\lambda 13168$ relative to O i $\lambda 11290$ , as well as the observed O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio, which diverges significantly from predictions for Ly $\beta$ fluorescence in an H ii region presented by Grandi [31]. As such, though O i $\lambda 8449$ is commonly observed arising from the broad-line regions of AGN due to Ly $\beta$ fluorescence and collisional excitation [32, 70, 65, e.g.,], its presence in the spectra of star-forming galaxies is not an indicator of the aforementioned processes.

Notably, we observe in our sample a strong correlation between the O i $\lambda 8449$ and H $\alpha$ line strengths, evidenced by the relatively narrow range of observed O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratios shown in Figure 4. This tight correlation between O i and H $\alpha$ emission can indeed arise due to Ly $\beta$ fluorescence, as suggested by de Graaff et al. [20] in the case of a large sample of LRDs. However, given that we have strongly ruled out contributions from Ly $\beta$ fluorescence in favor of stellar continuum fluorescence, we highlight the necessity of constraining the O i $\lambda 8449$ production mechanism using both the O i $\lambda 11290$ and O i $\lambda 13168$ emission lines, given that a tight O i $\lambda 8449$ -H $\alpha$ correlation is not itself an indicator of Ly $\beta$ fluorescence.

Additionally, the detection of a permitted oxygen line in star-forming galaxies may initially lead to the assumption that this line comes from recombination. In this case, the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio would serve as a valuable metallicity indicator, since recombination-line metallicities have a weaker temperature dependence than those derived from the “direct” $T_{e}$ -based method [53, e.g.,], and are less susceptible to the effects of temperature fluctuations that would bias derived abundances [61, 80, e.g.,]. However, the non-detection of several other recombination lines such as O i $\lambda 7776$ , as well as the extremely low theoretical recombination-based O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio derived in Section IV.1 securely rule out recombination as the dominant process contributing to O i. Thus, O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ may be of limited use as a metallicity indicator for star-forming galaxies, and will certainly lead to unreasonable estimates if recombination is assumed to be the dominant mechanism [76].

Beyond the local Universe, the O i $\lambda 8449$ feature has now been observed with JWST in a variety of sources. In the Sunburst Arc at $z=2.37$ , Choe et al. [17] measured this line in a highly magnified source referred to as “Godzilla,” noting a highly elevated O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\beta$ ratio of $20.75\pm 0.15\%$ . This ratio is much larger than the values that we find to be characteristic of our sample of star-forming galaxies. Indeed, Choe et al. [17] suggest that the mechanism powering O i $\lambda 8449$ in Godzilla is Ly $\beta$ fluorescence, resembling closely the processes occurring in the Weigelt blobs in the luminous blue variable $\eta$ Car [41]. Vanzella et al. [82] also find evidence of PAR due to Ly $\alpha$ in this object, detecting the emission of several pumped Fe lines. Thus, the production mechanism for O i $\lambda 8449$ in Godzilla differs from what we observe in our sample, likely due to the extreme conditions (i.e., $\gtrsim$ $10^{6}\rm\ cm^{-3}$ ) found in this source. Because this emission line is now more routinely observed in high-redshift sources thanks to the exquisite sensitivity of JWST, it is critical to understand its production mechanism in each class of object, given that the different O i production mechanisms are indicators of vastly different physical conditions.

We note that in the analysis of Choe et al. [17], they also present rest-UV observations covering the O i $\lambda 1302,\lambda 1305,\lambda 1306$ triplet, observed in both emission and absorption. Though we measure the O i emission to be weaker in typical star-forming galaxies than in Godzilla (as quantified by the O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratio), the complex O i and Si ii profiles presented by Choe et al. [17] may highlight the general need for a more careful treatment of both emission and absorption components when fitting this feature in down-the-barrel observations of $z\sim 2$ galaxies [75, 23, 64, e.g.,]. Overall, this work highlights the valuable constraints on the production mechanism of O i $\lambda 8449$ obtained from measuring the O i $\lambda 11290$ and O i $\lambda 13168$ lines. With these constraints, it is possible to distinguish between a variety of distinct physical conditions that all produce the O i $\lambda 8449$ emission line.

## VI Conclusions

We present detections of the permitted O i $\lambda 8449$ line in 14 star-forming galaxies, as well as stacks comprising 58 galaxies from the AURORA survey. We explore evidence for four candidate excitation mechanisms: recombination, collisional excitation, Ly $\beta$ fluorescence, and stellar continuum fluorescence. We determine that stellar continuum fluorescence provides the most compelling explanation for the production of this emission line. Our primary conclusions are as follows:

- 1. The O i $\lambda 8449$ line is present in the stack of all galaxies in which the line was not individually detected (Stack-NonDet). As such, it is likely that O i $\lambda 8449$ emission (at $\sim$ 0.5% the strength of H $\alpha$ ) is a ubiquitous feature of star-forming galaxies at $z\sim 2$ . Additionally, the detection of this line in the more nearby Universe ( $z<0.1619$ ) in 1602 galaxies from DESI DR1 as well as local H ii regions from the CHAOS survey suggests that this fluorescent line is a common feature of star-forming galaxies across cosmic time.

- 2. We determine that the dominant production mechanism for O i $\lambda 8449$ in star-forming galaxies is stellar continuum fluorescence, as evidenced by the detection of O i $\lambda 13168$ . We estimate that recombination, collisional excitation, and Ly $\beta$ fluorescence contribute $1.0\%\pm 0.2\%$ , $0.16\%\pm 0.09\%$ , and $0.81\%\pm 0.08\%$ to the O i $\lambda 8449$ emission, respectively.

- 3. Simultaneously modeling O i $\lambda 8449$ , O i $\lambda 11290$ , and O i $\lambda 13168$ is challenging when using the isobaric Cloudy models that we present in this analysis. Improving upon these simplified models with a more complex density profile and placing tighter constraints on ISM turbulence may serve as valuable avenues for improving predictions of the relative strengths of these three lines.

JWST observations continue to enable the characterization of the $z\sim 2$ star-forming galaxy population in unprecedented detail through the measurement of faint spectroscopic features. Characterizing and accurately interpreting the origins of these features is critical for building a comprehensive picture of the conditions in the ISM. In the case of O i $\lambda 8449$ , because this feature is seen in a variety of sources and can be produced by very different conditions, constraining the production mechanism for this line in star-forming galaxies is valuable for ruling out the extreme and unusual conditions that would be required for processes such as Ly $\beta$ PAR to contribute. Additionally, because faint metal recombination lines are often used to derive metallicities with little dependence on density or temperature, accurately distinguishing between recombination and contributions from fluorescence is critical for deriving robust metal abundances [80, e.g.,]. In summary, though future work remains to be done to better reproduce the observed O i line emission strengths in the AURORA sample, stellar continuum fluorescence offers the most compelling explanation for the presence of this line in star-forming galaxies.

## Appendix A Varying Cloudy Oxygen abundances

In Figure 7, we show the effects of varying the nebular oxygen abundance on the various O i line ratios that we consider. The subplots in the left column show the same model curves as those presented in Figure 6. We additionally consider oxygen abundances of 0.5 $\rm Z_{\odot}$ and 1.0 $\rm Z_{\odot}$ . Overall, varying the nebular metallicity over this specified range does not have a significant impact on the predicted O i $\lambda 8449$ /H $\alpha$ ratios. In principle, a Monte Carlo radiative transfer calculation would be required to robustly capture the line fluorescence channels. However, we present the Cloudy model predictions at different oxygen abundances as a rough estimate of the effect of varying metallicity.

## Abstract

We present the discovery of supernova (SN) Ares, a strongly lensed supernova at $z_{\rm spec}=1.276\pm 0.002$ in a massive, triply imaged host galaxy behind the MACS J0308.9+2645 galaxy cluster. JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy spanning the rest-frame optical to NIR of Ares reveals helium features at 5876 Å, 7065 Å, and 10830 Å as well as H $\alpha$ and Pa $\beta$ . A comparison to local core-collapse SN spectra and light curves leads to a classification of SN Ares as a Type IIb supernova, the highest-redshift member of its class spectroscopically identified. A comparison to local SN IIb light curves provides a phase estimate for the spectrum of $34_{-9}^{+10}$ rest-frame days post-radioactive peak, providing a unique view into a high-redshift stripped-envelope supernova in its late-photospheric evolution. A lens model of the cluster constructed using recent JWST data indicates that SN Ares is the first image to arrive and will reappear in two future images near the center of the cluster plane in $\gtrsim 70$ years, with predicted magnifications of $\sim 5$ x and $\sim 1.5$ x. Planned JWST/NIRSpec Multi-Object Spectroscopy of the cluster will allow for more detailed modeling of the lensed system for tighter constraints on the time delay and magnifications, as well as a template spectrum at the location of SN Ares.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

The phenomenon of strong gravitational lensing occurs when a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or galaxy cluster, distorts the light from a background source. This results in multiple magnified images appearing at different times (for reviews on galaxy- and cluster-scale strong lensing, see Shajib et al. 97 and Natarajan et al. 75). The offset in arrival time between images can be anywhere from hours to decades depending on the mass of the foreground lens and the geometry of the system, with cluster-scale lenses typically producing longer time delays [77]. The absolute and relative size of these delays is related to the physical scale of the Universe through the geometric configuration of the lens and background source [62].

Due to the direct relationship between these delays and geometric distance, a measurement of the offset in image arrival times leads to constraints on cosmological parameters such as the local expansion rate of the Universe, $H_{0}$ [89]. The use of these delays for cosmological measurements is known as “time-delay cosmography” [89, 107, 108] and has found great success with galaxy-scale lensed quasar systems [113, 104, 105, 106]. Recently, strongly lensed supernovae (SNe) have emerged as incredible tools for time-delay cosmography as well. So far, four measurements of $H_{0}$ have been made with strongly lensed SNe (Refsdal, H0pe, Encore, and 2025wny), finding $H_{0}$ values that span the current cosmological tension, from $65\,\rm{kms^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ to $76\,\rm{kms^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ [56, 46, 82, 85, 101, 12, 52, 73, 95]. The advantages of lensed SN systems in particular are clear: the lensed SNe have predictable light curves with distinct features (such as a radioactive peak) that simplify time-delay measurements; they require short observing campaigns of weeks to months; they are resistant to the effects of chromatic microlensing [40, 86, 49], and they fade on timescales which allow for template observations after the SN has faded [27]. Regardless of whether the source is a lensed SN or quasar, cluster-scale systems possess an advantage over galaxy-scale systems in that they include multiple background sources across redshifts, which helps alleviate the mass sheet degeneracy uncertainty at the price of a more complex model [14]. Conversely, clusters are not dynamically relaxed systems. As such, traditional dynamical methods cannot be used to help constrain the multi-peaked mass model and reduce mass-sheet degeneracy. Furthermore, cluster environments and line of sight objects which contribute to the lensing potential are likely to be complex, requiring a dedicated analysis. Finally, for simply-parametrized models, residual errors in predicting image positions are of order tenths of arcseconds [12], indicating that structures with Einstein radii smaller than this are not fully accounted for. In order to better understand their relative strengths and weaknesses, it is crucial to continue building samples of strongly lensed SNe at both the galaxy and cluster scales.

Apart from their usefulness for cosmology, strongly lensed SNe also allow for unprecedented studies of high-redshift SN physics. Such studies elucidate the evolution in SN and SN progenitor properties, as well as inform us on how chemical enrichment has occurred over cosmic time. Without the magnification afforded by lensing, however, it would be impossible to detect (much less comprehensively analyze) certain classes of SNe out to high redshifts. For example, SN Refsdal (a 1987A-like core-collapse SN at $z=1.49$ ), would have had a peak magnitude $m_{V}>27$ mag and would have been undetectable by HST without its $\mu=15$ magnification [55]. Furthermore, it would have been impossible for HST to have obtained a spectrum that could even classify this event at all. Similarly, the recently discovered Type II SN Eos at $z=5.13$ , would have been completely undetectable without the $\sim 30$ x boost ( $\sim 4$ magnitudes) in brightness afforded by lensing [2, 24, 5]. Not only did lensing allow for its discovery, a remarkably high signal-to-noise spectrum obtained with JWST/NIRSpec allowed for a direct measurement of the Fe II 5018 Å absorption component, directly confirming the expectation based on its host galaxy that it was formed in a low-metallicity environment. Another recent strongly lensed SN at $z\approx 2$ , 2025wny, a member of an intrinsically bright sub-class known as superluminous SNe [38], was also magnified by $\mu\gtrsim 20$ , allowing for high signal-to-noise spectroscopy from multiple ground based observatories in addition to space-based resources [53, 44, 61]. Although this SN is intrinsically bright ( $M_{\rm UV}\lesssim-21$ mag), the massive boost by lensing allows for a much more detailed study than would be possible otherwise. These recent discoveries show how strongly lensed SNe can be simultaneously valuable for precision time-delay cosmography as well as studies of high-redshift SN physics, greatly extending the parameter space in terms of SN type and brightness for which we can make spectroscopic observations. Although we can expect many more spectroscopically confirmed SNe in the field with Roman, studies such as these that probe fundamental spectroscopic properties at high redshifts will only remain possible with JWST observations of lensed SNe.

Here, we present the discovery and JWST + HST follow-up of SN Ares, a strongly lensed, core-collapse SN at $z=1.276$ . In Section II, we present the spectrophotometric dataset of SN Ares. The lens model analysis of MACS J0308.9+2645 and the resulting $\sim 70$ -year reapperances of SN Ares is discussed in Section III. In Section IV, we show the JWST/NIRSpec FS observation of SN Ares and the resulting classification as an SN IIb. We combine this classification with our photometric dataset to form our best estimate for the phase of the SN in Section V. Finally, in Section VI we conclude about the future possible use of SN Ares as an incredibly precise long-baseline time delay experiment, as well as the takeaways for high-redshift SN physics.

## II Observations

SN Ares ( $\alpha=03^{\mathrm{h}}08^{\mathrm{m}}53^{\mathrm{s}}_{{}^{\centerdot}}418$ , $\delta=+26^{\circ}45^{\prime}58\farcs 63$ , J2000) was discovered in JWST/NIRCam imaging acquired on 2025 August 23 (UTC dates are used throughout, MJD times of observations found in Table 1) by the Vast Exploration for Nascent, Unexplored Sources [36, VENUS, Cycle 4 GO: PID 6882;] collaboration in the MACS J0308.9+2645 cluster field behind a bright foreground star in a large star-forming and multiply imaged host. A color image of this field constructed with HST and JWST data is shown in Figure 1.

### II.1 JWST Data

The JWST/NIRCam discovery data of SN Ares taken by VENUS consists of ten filters: (F090W, F115W, F150W, F200W, F210M, F277W, F300M, F356W, F410M, amd F444W). NIRCam images in the F115W, F150W, F200W, F250M, F300M, and F410M filters were taken prior to the explosion of SN Ares on 2025 February 4 [114, 1, Cycle 3 GO: PID 5293;], which are used as template images for our analysis. The imaging is reduced with the standard VENUS grizli infrastructure [17], used by all VENUS studies [74, 42, 25, 115, 3, 6, e.g.,], which applies the level-2 detector calibrations with corrections for snowball artifacts, wisp features, and $1/f$ noise. This pipeline also aligns the images to the Gaia DR3 frame and produces level-3 drizzled images (whereby all dithered exposures are combined into a single mosaic) on a common reference frame, thus enabling robust difference imaging. Cutouts of the science, template, and difference images from this pipeline procedure are presented in Figure 2. We performed aperture photometry with local background subtraction and aperture corrections using the space_phot package [88], the results of which are shown in Table 1.

Following the discovery of SN Ares, a JWST Director’s Discretionary Time program was approved to obtain an epoch of F115W/F444W NIRCam imaging and a NIRSpec spectrum (JWST DDT PID: 9478). These data were obtained on 2025 September 23, an observer-frame month from the discovery epoch. NIRSpec fixed-slit PRISM/CLEAR spectroscopy of SN Ares was obtained through the S200A1 aperture in a five-point nod pattern, for a total exposure time of 4012 s. We retrieved the stage-1 products from MAST, where they were processed with the JWST11 1 https://github.com/spacetelescope/jwst pipeline [20, version 1.20.2;] routines for saturation flagging, bias and dark subtraction, jump detection, and ramp fitting.

We reduced these products with msaexp22 2 https://github.com/gbrammer/msaexp [18, version 0.6.17;], which calls the JWST pipeline routines for wavelength calibration, slit rectification, flat-field correction, and flux calibration. We constructed a sky background model by fitting a cubic spline in wavelength to slit pixels unaffected by SN and host galaxy light. The five exposures were then drizzle-combined onto a common rectified grid, and we performed an optimal point-source extraction. Finally, we applied an additional local background subtraction to remove residual background emission from the host galaxy. The reduced spectrum is shown in Figure 3.

### II.2 HST Data

Further HST/WFC3 UVIS/IR observations in the F814W, F110W, and F160W filters of the SN Ares field were obtained following the JWST discovery [87, HST GO PID: 17474,]. Due to a combination of the lower resolution of HST and contamination from the nearby foreground star, these data produced only upper limits on the SN Ares light curve evolution. We present a discussion of these data and present upper limits for F160W in Appendix A. Future template observations matching more closely to the position angle of our observations may allow for a detection, however, such observations are currently not planned.

## III Lens model and predictions

In order to estimate the uncertainty in future arrival times of the SN Ares images, we rely on three independent lens models of MACS J0308.9+2645. We note that these lens model predictions will be greatly improved when we take scheduled JWST/NIRSpec Multi-Object Spectroscopcy (MOS) observations of the field in early 2027.

The first model uses a collection of dual Pseudo Isothermal Elliptical mass distributions (dPIE) using Lenstool [58]. Cluster members were identified using a double red sequence method and the lens model is constrained by 48 multiple images belonging to 15 independent families. Two of these families have spectroscopic redshifts while the rest rely on tight photometric redshifts from the 17 combined HST and JWST filters. The lens model has an RMS of $0.^{\prime\prime}66$ and was used to estimate $\mu=5.6\pm 0.5$ for SN Ares. According to the lens model, we are observing the first of three arrivals of SN Ares. We note that the arrival order is defined by the geometry of the lensing system and is not sensitive to a particular model. With $H_{0}=70\,\rm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ , the second arrival is predicted in $70\pm 1$ years with $\mu=4.9\pm 0.1$ , while the third and last arrival is predicted in $73\pm 1$ years with $\mu=1.5\pm 0.1$ . A difference of 3 $\rm{kms^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ in the value of $H_{0}$ leads roughly to a difference of 5 years in the time delays (with a lower value of $H_{0}$ leading to a higher time delay). A final monitoring campaign must cover both uncertainty from the lens models and uncertainty in the cosmological model. Over time, as both lens model methods and constraints on MACS J0308.9+2645 improve, both sources of uncertainty will certainly be better constrained, thus tightening the window over which the cluster must be monitored. A detailed description of the method used to construct this lens model will be presented in Resseguier et al. (in prep.).

Another strong lens mass model constructed with the glafic software [76, 78] predicts similar magnifications and time delays, including a magnification of $\mu=4.7\pm 0.3$ for SN Ares, a second arrival in $72\pm 2$ years, and a third arrival in $77\pm 4$ years, again assuming $H_{0}=70\,\rm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$ . The lens model will be presented in M. Oguri et al. (in prep.).

A third parametric, JWST-based SL mass model of MACS J0308.9+2645 was derived with the code AstroLensPy [3, ALP;], which is a python implementation of the Zitrin et al. [117] analytic method. It is constrained with 45 multiple images of 21 sources, two of which have spectroscopic redshifts, and achieves a lens-plane average image reproduction error $\Delta_{\mathrm{RMS}}=0.37^{\prime\prime}$ . According to this model, SN Ares is magnified by a factor $\mu=4.6\pm 0.4$ , in agreement with both the lenstool and glafic models at $1\sigma$ , and will re-appear in $76.4\pm 0.3$ yr, and again in $79.1\pm 0.4$ yr. This model will be published in Allingham et al. (in prep.).

## IV Spectroscopic classification

In Figure 3 we show the NIRSpec spectrum of SN Ares from rest-frame $4000$ – $20000$ Å, where there is sufficient signal-to-noise for spectroscopic comparison. We measured the redshift for SN Ares from a 1D spectrum extracted with a boxcar aperture centered on the host galaxy. We modeled its continuum and spectral lines with additional routines in msaexp [18]. Several strong emission lines fix the redshift, including [O II] $\lambda 3727$ , H $\beta$ + [O III] $\lambda 5007$ , H $\alpha$ +[N II] $\lambda\lambda$ 6548,6583, [S II] $\lambda\lambda$ 6717,6731, He I $\lambda$ 10830, Pa $\beta$ , and Pa $\alpha$ . The best fit is z = $1.276\pm 0.002$ . We show the spectrum used for this fit in Appendix B. For classification, we favor the Next Generation SuperFit (NGSF) code, as it fits a host continuum contribution to the spectrum jointly with the SN templates [48, 41]. This is useful in the case of SN Ares, which has host contribution in its spectrum even after our best local host subtraction. From this, we found that the best classification is that of a Type IIb SN (SN IIb), a partially stripped massive star explosion with a far smaller hydrogen envelope than nonstripped core-collapse SN progenitors. This smaller envelope results in an early spectroscopic evolution similar to SNe IIP/L which then transitions to a spectroscopic series more similar to SNe Ib/c [19]. Since H $\alpha$ is detected, it is immediately apparent that SN Ares is not an SN Ib/c, which lack signatures of hydrogen entirely.

The main diagnostic that favors SN Ares as an SN IIb rather than a SN IIP/L, is the existence and strength of the helium features, including the He I $5876$ Å and $7065$ Å features that lie to either side of the H $\alpha$ profile. The existence of lines at these wavelengths is not necessarily an immediate indication of an SN IIb classification, as both may appear at later times for SNe IIP/L, with a Na I doublet also contributing to the blue emission feature. However, the large ratio of the $5876$ Å feature to H $\alpha$ strength strongly favors an SN IIb classification, rather than that of an SN IIP/L. Even in late times, the He I (mixed with Na I) $5876$ Å and He I $7065$ Å features are much weaker relative to H $\alpha$ than we observe for SN Ares. The same argument is true for the size of the He I $10830$ Å to Pa $\beta$ line ratio, which is much higher for SN Ares than would be expected of a typical SN II, except perhaps at nebular times. And if SN Ares were a late-time SN IIP/L, there would be other emergent forbidden lines ([O I], [Ca II], [Fe II]) that are absent from the spectrum.

With the classification of SN Ares as an SN IIb, we now attempt to find its best match to well-studied, local analogs. To achieve this, we modify NGSF to contain a larger sample of template spectra across a wide phase range. We add all available spectra from the Open Supernova Catalog (OSC) for the SNe IIb that are included in the most recent NGSF template release [47, 41]. These include: 1993J, 1996cb, 2001ig, 2008aq, 2008ax, 2011dh, 2011fu, 2012dy, 2013cu, 2013df, and PS15bgt (with added spectra and sources shown in Table 2). We fit NGSF in the range of $5000$ Å to $7800$ Å to compare based only on the He I $5876~$ Å, $7065~$ Å, and H $\alpha$ line region, the shape of which strongly correlates with spectral phase. To approximate the resolution of the NIRSpec spectrum, we set the binning of these spectra to 50 Å; however, we note that such a comparison is coarse and thus we only use this as a qualitative approach to identify possible best analogs to SN Ares. Our approach yields best matches to the well-studied SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, and SN 2011fu, appearing to be in a phase range of + $15$ - $35$ days post-radioactive peak. We show a few of the closest comparisons, normalized to the median of their continuua between $7400$ to $7650$ Å, in Figure 4. Overall, the H $\alpha$ line appears stronger for SN Ares compared to these other SNe, while the Ca II triplet (at $8500$ Å) appears weaker. Since the SN and host galaxy fill a large fraction of the slit, the sky background was estimated from a small region. We believe imperfect sky subtraction therefore affects flux levels, particularly at the bluest wavelengths where the SN signal is weakest. This flux discrepancy can be seen in the comparison figure, where SN Ares appears to follow the same continuum shape as the comparisons but is overbright on the blue end. Due to this, we do not speculate on differences in any lines blueward of the He I $5876$ Å feature.

## V Estimate of phase

*Figure 4: Comparison of well-matching spectra, choices of comparison for which are from an NGSF comparison of SN Ares to the best-observed local SNe IIb. The SNe are each normalized to their continuua at $7400-7650$ Å rest-frame. The spectrum includes a local background subtraction; residual host contamination is likely the cause of the divergent blue continuum between SN Ares and the comparison SNe. Each SN shows a different ratio between the He I 5876, 7065 Å and H $\alpha$ emission lines. SN Ares appears to have both a slightly stronger H $\alpha$ and weaker Ca II triplet (8498 Å, 8542 Å, and 8662 Å) than the comparison SNe IIb, with the most comparable being SN 1993J. This, along with a seemingly stronger H $\alpha$ profile may point to a less-stripped progenitor hydrogen envelope for SN Ares, although the strengths of these lines are degenerate with phase.*

For both the purposes of investigating SN physics and utilizing SN Ares as a future time-delay cosmography probe, it is crucial to estimate its phase at the time of our observations. However, unlike SNe Ia, which exhibit a fairly standard light curve evolution, core-collapse SNe display significant heterogeneity in both light curve and spectroscopic evolution, making phase estimation difficult. In Section V.1, we estimate the phase of SN Ares for this detected image by comparing against a large sample of stripped-envelope SN spectral templates. We further compare against the best-studied local SN IIb sample and attempt to find our best spectroscopic analogs against which to compare. In Section V.2, we use these analogs as light curve templates, as well as templates constructed from the SN IIb population, with which we can more accurately measure the phase.

### V.1 Spectroscopic comparison

Our first approach is to compare against the Carnegie Supernova Project (CSP) stripped-envelope supernova (SESN) templates in the NIR presented by Shahbandeh et al. [96]. We specifically utilize the helium-rich templates which were constructed using principal component analysis of both SN IIb and SN Ib NIR spectra, which were shown to be identical up to a fourth order component. These templates are sampled at a 1 day temporal resolution, from -5 days pre-radioactive peak to +80 days post-peak, resulting in 86 templates total. To compare against these templates, we isolate the rest-frame $8200$ – $12000$ Å region, encompassing the Ca II triplet and the He I/Pa $\gamma$ blend near $10830$ Å. We use this wavelength region specifically, as the templates show the greatest variation in these two features across the phase range, with the Ca II feature growing in strength relative to the continuum over time, while He I appears to slightly weaken in comparison. To estimate an uncertainty on phase, we calculate a $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ value for the difference between the template and SN Ares spectra, after normalizing each to the 9200 – 9750 Å continuum region. Due to the one-day cadence on the spectral templates, we then simply interpolate through these values to find the phases at which $\chi^{2}_{\nu}=\chi^{2}_{\nu,min}+1$ to recover our $1\sigma$ uncertainties. For this, we use a piecewise cubic hermite interpolating polynomial, employed through the scipy package [111]. We find a spectroscopic phase (relative to B-band peak) of $13\pm 12$ days, with $\chi^{2}_{\nu,\,\rm min}\approx 2.4$ . We show the best-matching $+13$ -day template along with an earlier and later template from Shahbandeh et al. [96] in the left panel of Figure 5. We show the equivalent CSP templates from the SN II population presented by Davis et al. [26] in the right panel for comparison. From the strong helium emission relative to Pa $\beta$ , the classificaton of SN Ares as an SN IIb is clear. Although the fits to the He-rich SESN templates are overall much better than to the more hydrogen rich SNe II, there are still some differences. For one, the Ca II to He I line ratio differs from the overall population, with the relative strengths of the two lines not perfectly aligning at any template phase. In particular, the Ca II complex strength seems most closely matched at earlier epochs, while the He I feature only begins to match at phases $>20$ days. Thus, fitting to only the He I feature favors a later phase estimate. It is also clear that the Pa $\beta$ line is stronger in SN Ares than the overall SESN population and more similar to the non-stripped SN II population, potentially indicating that SN Ares retains more of its hydrogen envelope than local SESNe on average. We therefore caution that our comparisons against best-matched spectroscopic analogs may be more accurate than this population-level comparison.

*Figure 5: Comparison of SN Ares versus the NIR templates from the helium-rich CSP SESN sample from Shahbandeh et al. [96] on the left and the SN II sample from Davis et al. [26] on the right. SN Ares clearly matches preferentially to the SESN templates, most starkly accentuated by the agreement in the He I feature. Even later time SN II templates still show strong disagreement with the SN Ares spectrum. The Pa $\beta$ feature does seem to match the SN II relative strength better, possibly indicating that SN Ares retained more of its hydrogen envelope than the low-redshift SESN analogs.*

As a further comparison, we turn to the best local analogs, SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, and SN 2011fu. We focus on the optical He I and H $\alpha$ line complex, since the relative strengths of these lines also vary by phase. For this analysis, we first fit and subtract the continuum around the region and then normalize to the median of the line region, which we define as being from $5600-7500$ Å. We use all available spectra from the OSC (references shown in Table 2) and fit for the $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ as with the CSP comparison. We require that the comparison spectra cover the full wavelength range of the line complex. We then estimate the best phase by identifying the minimum $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ value through a polynomial fit between the phases and $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ values (after removing $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ values above 10) using numpy and again define our $1\sigma$ uncertainties as based on where $\chi^{2}_{\nu}=\chi^{2}_{\nu,\,\rm min}+1$ . From this, we find phase estimates of $30\pm 19$ , $23\pm 20$ , and $15\pm 26$ days for the three SNe, respectively. Taking the weighted average of these values, we obtain a phase estimate of $24\pm 12$ days, a wide range but in agreement with the NIR CSP comparison. In particular, this analysis favors a later phase estimate, such as we obtain in the NIR when we only fit the He I feature. We find that SN 1993J appears to be the closest analog to SN Ares of the three, with the lowest $\chi^{2}_{\nu,\,\rm min}$ minimum of 1.9.

### V.2 Light curve fits

To estimate the phase of SN Ares photometrically, we apply a similar methodology as for the spectroscopic comparison: fitting against both population-level templates and the best local analog SNe IIb. For the latter, we compare the SN Ares photometry to the previously discussed SNe IIb 1993J, 2011dh, and 2011fu. The comparison light curves are corrected for Milky Way and host-galaxy extinction before fitting. We adopt total color excesses of $E(B-V)=0.194$ mag for SN 1993J [63], $E(B-V)=0.07$ mag for SN 2011dh [30], and $E(B-V)=0.10$ mag for SN 2011fu [71]. The SN Ares photometry are corrected for a fixed Milky Way foreground extinction of $E(B-V)_{\rm MW}=0.184$ mag [94, 93] assuming $R_{V}=3.1$ and a Fitzpatrick extinction law [32]. Any additional extinction along the line of sight to Ares is added as a free parameter in our light curve fitting methodology. The sources of the photometry for each comparison SN were obtained by searching the OSC, with individual sources and bands described in Table 3.

For each comparison SN, we construct Gaussian-process (GP) interpolations of the available light curves. The GP model uses a Matérn- $3/2$ covariance kernel and includes the reported photometric uncertainties from the OSC. The time of the main radioactive $B$ -band maximum is determined from the GP interpolation of the $B$ -band light curve around the radioactive peak.

Because the observed and rest-frame filters are not identical, cross-filter corrections are calculated directly from the observed spectrum of SN Ares. Before calculating these corrections, the spectrum is corrected for Milky Way extinction. Synthetic photometry through the appropriate observer- and rest-frame filter transmission curves is then used to determine the cross-filter correction for each filter pair. We include an additional uncertainty of $0.10$ mag in quadrature to account for systematic uncertainty associated with deriving the cross-filter corrections from a single spectrum, which is based on the largest cross-filter correction value we obtain in our methodology.

For a photometric observation at MJD $t_{i}$ , the rest-frame phase in the comparison-SN light curve is

$$ \phi_{i}=\phi_{\rm ref}+\frac{t_{i}-t_{\rm ref}}{1+z_{\rm Ares}}, $$

where $z_{\rm Ares}=1.276$ and $t_{\rm ref}$ is the date of the spectrum observation. Thus, the fitted phase reported throughout the analysis corresponds specifically to the phase of SN Ares at the second JWST epoch.

The model contains four free parameters: the reference phase $\phi_{\rm ref}$ , a common magnitude offset $\Delta m$ that combines both the effect of magnification and the redshift-dependent K correction, the host-galaxy color excess of SN Ares $E(B-V)_{\rm host}$ , and an additional intrinsic-scatter term $\sigma_{\rm int}$ . For an observation in filter $f$ , the model magnitude is schematically

$$ m_{{\rm model},i}=m_{{\rm GP},f}(\phi_{i})+\Delta m+K_{f}+A_{f}, $$

where $m_{{\rm GP},f}$ is the GP-interpolated comparison-SN magnitude, $K_{f}$ is the spectrum-derived cross-filter correction, and $A_{f}$ is the extinction in the corresponding rest-frame band.

The likelihood is evaluated using

$$ \ln{\cal L}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[\ln(2\pi\sigma_{i}^{2})+\frac{(m_{i}-m_{{\rm model},i})^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right], $$

with

$$ \sigma_{i}^{2}=\sigma_{m,i}^{2}+\sigma_{{\rm GP},i}^{2}+\sigma_{K}^{2}+\sigma_{\rm int}^{2}, $$

where $\sigma_{K}=0.10$ mag.

For SN 1993J, the light curve contains an extended late-time decline that can produce a secondary, weakly constrained phase solution. To prevent this solution from generating an artificial long tail in the phase posterior, we restrict the phase at the second JWST epoch to $-10<\phi_{B,\,\max}<60$ rest-frame days relative to the radioactive $B$ -band maximum. We additionally impose a weak half-normal regularization on the intrinsic-scatter parameter, with characteristic scale $0.15$ mag and $\sigma_{\rm int}<0.35$ mag. Both of these phase restrictions are implemented to prevent poor late-time matches from being accommodated simply by an inflated intrinsic scatter or from very uncertain GP fits. These choices on the prior are also informed by the spectroscopic phase estimates previously described, which strongly disfavor a very early or late phase.

Posterior distributions are sampled using the affine-invariant MCMC sampler implemented in the emcee package [33]. We characterize each fitted parameter by the posterior median and report uncertainties based on the 68th percentile confidence intervals. We find that the best-fit individual comparison is to SN 1993J, with a $\chi^{2}_{\nu}$ close to unity.

For our population-level comparison, we rely on the SN IIb GP templates provided by Khakpash et al. [57]. These templates were constructed using the total sample of SNe IIb provided by the OSC and is therefore not independent of our previous analyses. Unfortunately, due to lack of data, these models do not include a K-band template. Thus, we only fit with the provided matching filters shown in Table 3 for our final phase estimate. We test the H-band template to check the decline rate consistency between our observations and the template, and find good agreement at the final estimated phase from the optical-only fit. We show the best-fit single comparison object, SN 1993J, and the population-level template fit in Figure 6.

From these template fits to SNe 1993J, 2011dh, 2011fu and the population-level templates, we recover a phase estimate for the second epoch of JWST data (e.g. our spectral phase) of $31_{-5}^{+11}$ , $34_{-5}^{+10}$ , $31_{-9}^{+13}$ , and $34_{-9}^{+10}$ days, respectively. Therefore we find strong consistency in our measured phase across our best three local analogs, as well as from the population as a whole. The posterior distributions (shown in Appendix C) overall seem to show asymmetric distributions on phase, often with a higher-phase mode. This skewed uncertainty is represented in our reported phases, and we note that all of our phase estimates are in $1\sigma$ agreement to our estimates from the spectral comparisons.

#### V.2.1 Peak $B$ -band magnitude of SN Ares

We additionally use the fitted magnitude offsets to estimate the intrinsic peak rest-frame $B$ -band absolute magnitude of SN Ares. Because the fitted magnitude offset is defined between the apparent light curves of SN Ares and each comparison SN, the intrinsic peak absolute magnitude of SN Ares is calculated as

$$ \begin{split}M_{B,\,\max}^{\rm Ares}&=m_{B,\,\max}^{\rm tpl,0}+\Delta m-\mathrm{DM}_{\rm Ares}\\
&\quad+2.5\log_{10}\mu+2.5\log_{10}(1+z).\end{split} $$

Here, $M_{B,\,\max}^{\rm Ares}$ is the intrinsic, unlensed absolute magnitude of SN Ares at rest-frame $B$ -band maximum, and $m_{B,\max}^{\rm tpl,0}$ is the extinction-corrected apparent $B$ -band peak magnitude of the comparison template. The parameter $\Delta m$ is the common magnitude offset obtained by fitting the template light curves to Ares, with positive values corresponding to a fainter source. The distance modulus is $\mathrm{DM}_{\rm Ares}=5\log_{10}(D_{L}/10\,\mathrm{pc})$ , where $D_{L}$ is the luminosity distance in the adopted cosmology, which at $z=1.276$ gives a distance modulus of approximately 44.76 mag. The magnification $\mu$ , which we take to be $5.6\pm 0.5$ from the Lenstool model, enters through $+2.5\log_{10}\mu$ and corresponds to a $\sim 1.9$ mag difference. Finally, $+2.5\log_{10}(1+z)$ corrects for the redshift-dependent K-correction at the SN Ares redshift. The Ares Milky Way extinction and cross-filter corrections have already been applied to the photometry, while the SN Ares host extinction is included explicitly in the light-curve model.

We propagate the uncertainty in the fitted magnitude offset together with the asymmetric uncertainty in the lensing magnification using Monte Carlo sampling, with uncertainties propagated to the $M_{B,\,\max}$ absolute magnitude estimates. In the Vega system (with AB, Vega offsets from Blanton and Roweis 15) these estimates for SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, and SN 2011fu are $-17.9_{-0.3}^{+0.2}$ , $-17.1_{-0.3}^{+0.2}$ , and $-17.4_{-0.4}^{+0.4}$ , respectively. These values are all well within the distribution of SN IIb peak magnitudes presented by Richardson et al. [90], where $\langle\rm{M}_{B}\rangle=17.0\pm 1.3$ mag. Using the magnification from the glafic model produces slightly brighter estimates, but still within expectations.

## VI Discussion & Conclusions

Our analysis of SN Ares demonstrates the success of targeted JWST observations of rich galaxy clusters for the discovery and detailed study of high-redshift SNe. At a spectroscopic redshift of $z=1.276$ , Ares provides an unprecedented view of a high-redshift SN IIb through simultaneous coverage of its rest-frame optical and near-infrared spectrum. The combination of this wavelength coverage, multiband photometry, and a multiply imaged host galaxy makes the system valuable both for investigating SN properties at high redshift and for high-precision time-delay cosmography.

The classification of SN Ares as an SN IIb is supported by the presence of hydrogen and helium features and their relative strengths. In particular, the optical He I features near $5876$ and $7065$ Å, together with the near-infrared He I feature near $10830$ Å, favor a helium-rich explosion that retains some hydrogen. Although these individual features also appear in regular SNe II at later times, their collective morphology and relative prominence are best-matched to an SN IIb classification. The absence of prominent forbidden lines expected from a substantially later-phase SN II further supports this interpretation.

In order to estimate the phase, we compare SN Ares to three local analogs: SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, and SN 2011fu, all chosen based on their spectroscopic similarities. Among the local comparison objects, SN 1993J provides the closest overall match, although SN Ares is still distinct. Compared to these analogs, SN Ares seems to possess stronger H $\alpha$ emission and a weaker Ca II near-infrared triplet, which could reflect differences in envelope structure, mass, and excitation, although these properties all also depend on phase. Residual host-galaxy emission may contribute to the observed H $\alpha$ profile, making differences in hydrogen envelope mass poorly constrained given the current dataset. A future JWST/NIRSpec MOS observation is scheduled for early 2027 (PID 4568), which will allow for a host spectrum to be obtained after the transient has faded. This will allow us to subtract the host spectrum directly at the location of SN Ares and will help distinguish intrinsic SN emission from contamination, enabling a more reliable comparison of the line profiles. The photometric comparisons consistently place the NIRSpec observation approximately one month after the B-band radioactive peak. Fits using SN 1993J, SN 2011dh, and SN 2011fu give median phases between $31$ and $34$ rest-frame days, consistent with a population-template estimate of $34^{+10}_{-9}$ days using published GP templates constructed from all SN IIb light curves from the OSC. Our spectroscopic estimates of phase are much broader but still support a late-photospheric interpretation.

After correcting for the model magnification, the inferred peak $B$ -band magnitudes span approximately $-17.1$ to $-17.9$ mag across the three individual comparisons. These estimates are consistent with the luminosity distribution of nearby SNe IIb and do not require an unusually luminous explosion. The magnification of approximately $\mu=5.6$ , corresponds to a brightness enhancement of about $1.9$ mag, which enables spectroscopic study of an event whose inferred luminosity lies within the local SN IIb distribution. Its broad resemblance to nearby analogs shows that familiar SN IIb spectral behavior can be identified at this redshift, although a single event cannot establish whether the population or its progenitor channels have evolved. Apart from any individual physical differences to local analogs; however, it is perhaps interesting to find an SN IIb among the limited ( $<10$ ) spectroscopically observed strongly lensed SN sample, given that rates of SNe IIb are relatively low in the local Universe [43, $\sim 7\%$ of SNe II,]. Given its similarity to SN 1993J, 2011dh, and 2011fu, which have all been shown to have binary progenitor systems, it is likely that SN Ares has a similar higher-multiplicity progenitor origin. SN Refsdal, a 1987A-like SN, arose from an even rarer progenitor system that also almost certainly had a multiplicity greater than one. Future spectroscopic observations of lensed SNe may show whether such a trend in higher multiplicity at higher redshfits exists, which may be expected given the predicted inverse relationship between multiplicity and metallicity. More spectroscopic observations of lensed SNe are needed to disentangle these rates, as the magnification is needed to detect such objects at these redshifts. For blank-field surveys without the benefit of magnification, SNe like Refsdal and Ares would likely have gone undetected or with spectrophotometric datasets that were insufficient for a correct classification.

In addition to the interesting physical nature of SN Ares, its potential use as a long-baseline time-delay cosmography probe is also of particular note. Our current best lens models predict future appearances of SN Ares in $\sim 73$ and $76$ years after the observed image. Additional spectroscopic redshifts for the multiply imaged systems which will be obtained in early 2027 will strengthen the lens constraints and help assess the stability of the predicted delays. Assuming that the delays remain on the order of 70 years, the SN Ares system has by far the highest predicted delays of any discovered lensed SN system so far. The reappearance of SN Ares, and other yet-to-be discovered long-baseline lensed SNe, will require dedicated monitoring observations from next-generation telescopes. For a telescope set to launch within the next few decades, such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory, guaranteeing the reappearance of SN Ares may require the capability to service the mission to extend its lifetime. Assuming we are able to catch its reappearance, it would be trivial to measure a negligible, $\ll 1\%$ uncertainty on the time delay for SN Ares given its planned final dataset. Since the uncertainty on the time delay is directly proportional to the uncertainty on measured cosmological parameters, SN Ares represents the possibility for the most precise single-step measurement of cosmology currently known. The usefulness of SN Ares for cosmology will be limited only by the systematics in the lens models themselves. Our understanding of cosmology and lens modeling in 70 years is impossible to predict but regardless, the reappearance of SN Ares will almost certainly be a scientifically rich event worth capturing.

## Appendix A HST Analysis

As mentioned in Section II, five HST/WFC3 F814W, F110W, and F160W observations of SN Ares were obtained following its discovery. Unfortunately, due to the bright nearby foreground star, these observations result in nondetections. We constrain the F160W flux of SN Ares using the five HST follow-up epochs and a pre-explosion template from the Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey [23, RELICS,]. We subtract a fitted empirical PSF model for the nearby bright foreground star from both the science and template images using space_phot [88]. The star-model amplitudes and centroids are refit while allowing for a varying local background. We correct the pedestal in the saved PSF models and apply a raised-cosine taper over their outermost three pixels to suppress discontinuities at the model boundaries. This process for the science image is shown in Figure 7.

The star-subtracted science and template images share a common pixel grid and flux calibration due to the VENUS reduction pipeline. We form direct differences without additional resampling or PSF-matching convolution. We attempted such a deconvolution method as well, which erturned similar results. We measure the flux at the fixed SN Ares position using forced PSF photometry with the empirical science-image PSF and fit within a five-pixel radius. The difference images after PSF subtraction are shown in Figure 8.

We propagate the science and template error maps in quadrature and empirically rescale the formal flux uncertainties using the robust scatter of forced measurements at 131 nearby control positions. We assess sensitivity to the adopted SN position, fitting radius, star-model pedestal correction, model-edge taper, and relative photometric scaling and alignment. The largest absolute change in the fitted flux across these checks is adopted as a systematic term and added in quadrature to the empirically rescaled statistical uncertainty. No epoch exceeds a nominal significance of $3\sigma$ . We present the related upper limits in Table 4. We attempt this same approach for the other filters and similarly find nondetections. Because SN Ares is expected to be much fainter in these bands than F160W, we do not include the upper limits, as they are uninformative. Wihtout contamination from the bright, nearby star, it is almost certain that SN Ares would have been detected in at least the first epoch of F160W, given its predicted brightness. A future template image that matches the PA of the science images could be used to produce a much cleaner difference image where possible detections could be made.
